blocks.label: pool-allocated node factory
blocks.py:
store = []                            # object pool as list
free = []                              # free-index stack
def alloc(val):
    if free: i = free.pop(); store[i].val = val
    else: store.append(Node(val)); i = len(store)-1
    return i
def release(i): free.append(i)         # dangling-index hygiene on caller

items.title: Josephus Survivor (general k,n)
items.statement: Simulate with std::list circularly AND derive the O(n) recurrence; verify both on n≤10⁵.

solutionCode.label: circular simulation, and the O(n) recurrence that replaces it
solutionCode.py:
def josephus_sim(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """Simulation over a circular list. O(n*k)."""
    people = list(range(n))
    idx = 0
    while len(people) > 1:
        idx = (idx + k - 1) % len(people)   # step k-1 forward from the current slot
        people.pop(idx)                     # idx now points at the successor
    return people[0]


def josephus_rec(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """Recurrence: J(1) = 0, J(n) = (J(n-1) + k) mod n. O(n) time, O(1) space."""
    ans = 0                            # 0-indexed survivor for n = 1
    for m in range(2, n + 1):
        ans = (ans + k) % m
    return ans

items.complexity: Simulation with a circular list: O(n*k) — you step k times per elimination. Recurrence: O(n) time, O(1) space. For n = 10^5 the recurrence is the only viable one.

followups.a: After the first person (at index k-1) is removed, n-1 remain and counting restarts at index k mod n. Solving the smaller problem gives a survivor index relative to that new start, so shifting it back by k and taking mod n converts it to the original numbering: J(n) = (J(n-1) + k) mod n, with J(1) = 0.

followups.q: Why simulate at all if the recurrence is O(n)?
followups.a: As a cross-check. The recurrence is easy to get off by one — 0- versus 1-indexed survivors are a classic slip — and the simulation is obviously correct by construction. Verify them against each other on small n, then ship the recurrence for large n. That is the discipline, not the simulation itself.

items.title: Polynomial Add + Multiply via Lists
items.statement: Terms sorted by exponent descending: add = merge-with-combine; multiply = accumulate shifted adds into result chain keeping order.
hints: Add = LC21 with exponent comparator + coefficient sum.
Multiply: insert each product term into sorted result (or bucket array when degrees small).

solutionCode.label: add is a merge with combine; multiply accumulates by exponent

items.complexity: Add: O(m + n), a single merge pass. Multiply: O(m*n) products, kept ordered by accumulating into a map keyed on exponent — O(m*n log(m*n)), or O(m*n + D) with a bucket array when the degree D is small.

followups.q: Why must cancelling terms be dropped rather than stored as zero?
followups.a: A zero-coefficient term is not part of the polynomial, and leaving it in breaks equality comparison, degree calculation, and any later multiply that would propagate meaningless zeros. (x+1) + (-x+1) is 2, not 0x + 2. Dropping them is a correctness requirement, not tidiness.

followups.q: When is the bucket array better than the map for multiply?
followups.a: When the maximum degree D is small relative to m*n. A bucket array is O(D) space with O(1) accumulation and no sort — the output comes out ordered for free. The map wins when degrees are sparse and huge, where an array of size D would dwarf the number of real terms.

items.title: std::list Splice Merge-Sort Benchmark
items.statement: Sort 10⁶ elements two ways: list.merge() bottom-up vs vector.sort(); report timings + explain crossover honestly.
hints: lst has member merge() using operator<.

solutionCode.label: bottom-up merge over a linked list, and the honest benchmark verdict

items.complexity: list::merge splices in O(1) per node with zero allocation; bottom-up list merge sort is O(n log n) with no data movement. vector::sort is also O(n log n) but moves data — and wins anyway on modern hardware because of cache locality.

followups.a: There essentially is not one for plain ints — vector::sort wins at every size above a few hundred elements, by roughly 5-10x at n = 10^6. The list only becomes competitive when elements are large and expensive to move, or when iterator stability across the sort is a hard requirement. Claiming the list wins because splicing is O(1) ignores that the constant on a cache miss is about 100x a register move.

followups.q: Why is bottom-up preferred over top-down for lists?
followups.a: Top-down needs the midpoint, which costs an O(n) walk at every level — turning O(n log n) into O(n log n) with a much worse constant, plus O(log n) stack. Bottom-up never searches for a midpoint: it merges runs of 1, then 2, then 4, carrying them in a small array of accumulators.

items.title: Design Skip List (map API)
items.statement: Implement insert/search/erase with randomized heights; stress against std::set on 10⁶ ops.
hints: height = count trailing ones of rng&mask.

solutionCode.label: probabilistic towers with an update[] predecessor stack

items.complexity: Expected O(log n) for search, insert and erase. Worst case O(n) — the height is random, so a pathological coin-flip run degrades it, unlike a balanced tree's hard guarantee.

followups.q: Why is the expected height O(log n)?
followups.a: A node reaches height h with probability 2^-(h-1), so the expected number of nodes at height h is n * 2^-(h-1). That drops below 1 once h exceeds log2(n) + 1, so the tallest tower is about log2 n. Each level halves the candidates, giving expected O(log n) search — the same shape as a balanced tree, achieved by coin flips rather than rotations.

followups.q: Expected versus worst case — be honest.
followups.a: A skip list gives no worst-case guarantee: an unlucky run of coin flips can make every node height 1, degrading to a sorted linked list at O(n). A red-black tree guarantees O(log n) always. Skip lists are chosen for simpler code and easier lock-free concurrency, not for better bounds — say that rather than claiming equivalence.

items.title: LRU Cache — O(1) splice edition
items.statement: Re-implement F029/L3-foundations LRU using std::list<Key> + unordered_map<Key,list::iterator>; touch = splice-to-front O(1).
hints: Map stores iterators — stability guaranteed by list.
Compare against hand-rolled DLL version aloud.

solutionCode.label: std::list for recency, map from key to its iterator

items.complexity: O(1) for get and put. splice moves a node between positions without allocating, and list iterators stay valid across every operation except erasure of the node they point at.

followups.q: Why can the map safely store list iterators?
followups.a: std::list guarantees iterator stability: inserting or erasing other elements never invalidates an iterator, because each node is independently allocated and nothing is relocated. The same map over a vector would be corrupted by the first reallocation. That guarantee is exactly why list is the right container here.

followups.q: Compare against a hand-rolled doubly linked list.
followups.a: Identical asymptotics and structure — std::list IS a doubly linked list. The hand-rolled version avoids the iterator wrapper and can pack key and value into the node, saving one indirection and some memory. The library version is shorter and harder to get wrong. Mention that splice is the operation doing the work in both, so the choice is about clarity, not speed.

items.title: Text Editor Buffer (gap-buffer vs list debate)
items.statement: Support cursor insert/delete/move on 10⁶-char doc. Defend chosen structure (gap buffer / piece table / linked lines) with operation-frequency argument.
hints: List-of-lines wins line ops, loses cursor micro-ops.
Piece-table powers real editors (VS Code) — name-drop correctly.
No code required; architecture defense graded.

solutionCode.label: a piece table sketch, and the operation-frequency argument
solutionCode.py:
class PieceTable:
    """The structure VS Code uses. The original buffer is IMMUTABLE; edits append
    to a second buffer and the document is an ordered list of (buffer, start, len).

    Why it wins for a 10^6-character document: its costs land on RARE operations
    (random offset lookup, O(pieces) here and O(log n) with a balanced index)
    while its wins land on FREQUENT ones -- localised edits never move existing
    text, undo is just restoring the piece list, and opening a file is zero-copy.

    A gap buffer (Emacs) is the alternative: O(1) insert at the cursor and fully
    contiguous storage, but moving the cursor far costs O(distance) and undo
    needs a separate log. Linked lines make line splices O(1) but turn
    within-line cursor movement into a cache-hostile pointer chase."""

    ORIGINAL, ADDED = 0, 1

    def __init__(self, text: str = ""):
        self.original = text
        self.added = ""
        self.pieces = [(self.ORIGINAL, 0, len(text))] if text else []

    def insert(self, offset: int, text: str) -> None:
        if not text:
            return
        fresh = (self.ADDED, len(self.added), len(text))
        self.added += text
        walked = 0
        for i, (buf, start, length) in enumerate(self.pieces):
            if walked + length >= offset:
                split = offset - walked
                left = (buf, start, split)
                right = (buf, start + split, length - split)
                repl = [p for p in (left, fresh, right) if p[2] > 0]
                self.pieces[i:i+1] = repl
                return
            walked += length
        self.pieces.append(fresh)

    def delete(self, offset: int, count: int) -> None:
        out, walked, remaining = [], 0, count
        for buf, start, length in self.pieces:
            if remaining <= 0 or walked + length <= offset:
                out.append((buf, start, length))
            elif walked >= offset + count:
                out.append((buf, start, length))
            else:
                keep_left = max(0, offset - walked)
                if keep_left:
                    out.append((buf, start, keep_left))
                drop = min(length - keep_left, remaining)
                remaining -= drop
                rest = length - keep_left - drop
                if rest > 0:
                    out.append((buf, start + keep_left + drop, rest))
            walked += length
        self.pieces = [p for p in out if p[2] > 0]

    def text(self) -> str:
        src = (self.original, self.added)
        return "".join(src[b][s:s+l] for b, s, l in self.pieces)

items.complexity: Gap buffer: O(1) amortised insert/delete at the cursor, O(distance) to move the cursor. Piece table: O(log n) insert with a balanced index, O(1) undo, never mutates the original buffer. Linked lines: O(1) line splice, O(line length) for cursor movement within a line.

followups.q: Give the operation-frequency argument in one breath.
followups.a: Cursor movement within a line happens thousands of times a minute, edits hundreds, line operations tens, far jumps a handful. So the structure should optimise localised edits and cheap traversal, and may pay for random offset lookup. That ranking is what selects the piece table over linked lines — not any single asymptotic.

followups.q: Why does the piece table make undo nearly free?
followups.a: Because no existing text is ever mutated — edits only append to the added buffer and rewrite the piece list. Undo restores a previous piece list, which is a small array of triples, not a document snapshot. A gap buffer has to journal the actual characters it overwrote.
